name: Hood River Event Site
waterType: River, mostly flat with some chop; deep close to shore
windDirection: Prevailing westerly Gorge thermal
description: The most consistently cited wing foil destination in the US. The Gorge's venturi effect (desert heat inland vs. cool coastal air) makes wind reliable almost all season, and river current adds extra glide. Gusty, with real river traffic to watch for — a beginner is better served nearby at 'the Hook.' Personal note from Will: I've been to Hood River twice, though the first trip was before I'd gotten into wing foiling — I mostly just watched people out on the water. The second time was a family trip and I hadn't brought gear, so I still didn't get out there. I've done a lot of research on this spot since, and actually planned a trip out this past summer, but the wind forecast wasn't cooperating enough to justify the cost, so I did something else in Oregon instead. Haven't sailed it myself yet, but it's on the list.
sourceNote: Research-sourced (2026-08-28), not yet confirmed firsthand — see project notes.

name: Crissy Field
waterType: Ocean chop/swell, strong tidal current, shipping traffic
windDirection: NNW-WNW, funneled through the Golden Gate
description: The Bay Area's most iconic launch, right at the Golden Gate — powerful, highly reliable summer thermal wind, but strong current and boat traffic make this an experienced-riders-only spot. Beginners should look toward Coyote Point or Berkeley instead. SF Wing Foil Academy operates lessons at this location, confirming it as a real, active launch.
sourceNote: Firsthand-verified (2026-09-02) — confirmed via SF Wing Foil Academy, see description.

name: Waddell Creek Beach

windDirection: Northwest (prevailing NW coastal thermal)
description: A legendary NorCal windsurf spot now drawing wing foilers too — real ocean swell, not flat water, plus a reef/rock bottom. Powerful and beautiful, but for experienced riders only.
sourceNote: Research-sourced (2026-08-28), not yet confirmed firsthand — see project notes. Coordinates corrected to the paid parking lot at 3600 Hwy 1, Davenport, per californiabeaches.com (2026-09-02).

MANTA Wind and Water Sports (chief instructor John Arthur) teaches wing foil lessons here, confirming it as a real, active launch.

Steady wind April through November. Kitty Hawk Kiteboarding runs lessons at this location, confirming it as a real, active launch.

name: Curry Hammock State Park
waterType: Flat, shallow water, with a sandbar about a quarter-mile east offering extra riding space. Watch for submerged rocks, urchins, and coralline algae near shore — foot protection recommended. Marine life (rays, small sharks, tarpon, bonefish) present.
windDirection: ENE through E to WSW
description: A well-known Florida Keys kiteboarding and wing foiling spot at the state park, with a big stretch of flat, shallow water and a nearby sandbar. Note the slippery marl mud at the waterline and watch for golf cart traffic crossing lines near the campground.
sourceNote: Firsthand-verified (2026-08-29) by Will.

name: Punta Popy
waterType: Sand beach with shallow reef both north and south of the sailing area — open water in between. Waves can be good for wave riding depending on swell orientation.
windDirection: NE and E (trade winds) — side-shore in this direction; best season roughly April through September
description: An advanced-only spot on a sandy beach in Las Terrenas, bordered by shallow reef to the north and south with open water in between — good wave riding depending on swell direction, but not a place to learn the basics. The reefs sit downwind of the sailing area, so a mistake here compounds: if you get in trouble, you're getting swept toward the hazard, not away from it. Know exactly where you are relative to both reefs at all times. Met Julian, a local kiteboarding and wing foiling instructor, while sailing here — didn't take a lesson from him, but he was generous with advice and pointers. Find him at wingfoil-lasterrenas.com.
sourceNote: Firsthand-verified (2026-08-29) by Will.

name: Sanibel Island Causeway
waterType: Mostly flat/protected water around the causeway islands; can build to light chop in stronger wind. Watch for current near the bridge pilings.
windDirection: Works in essentially any direction thanks to the causeway's multiple islands/orientations — a go-to when the wind direction doesn't suit the Naples beaches (e.g. east wind, which is offshore in Naples)
skillLevel: All levels, with a caution around bridge-piling current
description: A well-known Gulf Coast kiteboarding and wing foiling spot on the islands of the Sanibel Causeway. Its varied island orientations mean it works in wind directions that don't suit the Naples beaches. Local tip: for gear, lessons, or repairs, Roy at Ace Performer (https://www.aceperformer.com/) is the go-to guy for wind sports in this area — new and used gear, lessons, and he's often out on the water with his truck if you need help or repairs mid-session. Parking at the Causeway is free — a nice contrast to the $5/hour lots at the Lighthouse and Gulfside City Beach Park.
sourceNote: Firsthand-verified (2026-08-29) by Will. Coordinates corrected via research to Causeway Islands Park — the causeway spans several islands, so the exact pin may vary by which one you launch from.

description: A popular Sanibel spot at the island's historic lighthouse, near the pass into San Carlos Bay. Parking here is also $5/hour.
sourceNote: Firsthand-verified (2026-08-29) by Will.

name: Grassy Flats Resort
waterType: Shallow flats/protected backcountry water — calm even in good wind, since a distant offshore reef breaks up the swell before it reaches the resort.
windDirection: NE, E, and ENE all work well here.
skillLevel: Beginner-friendly — the reef-protected calm water makes this one of the more forgiving spots on this list even when the wind is genuinely up
description: A true one-stop destination for wing foiling and kiteboarding at a Florida Keys resort in Marathon — gear rentals, lessons, and jet ski assist all on site, plus a restaurant, a small health-focused cafe, and hotel rooms for anyone who wants to make a full trip of it. Good beginner-quality conditions since a reef far offshore keeps the water calm even on solid wind days. (grassyflats.com)
sourceNote: Firsthand-verified (2026-08-29) by Will.

name: Cabarete Bay
waterType: Mixed — flatter water close in, with wave/swell further out; consistent cross-shore trade winds.
windDirection: Cross-shore trade winds, typically E/ESE
skillLevel: Intermediate+ for the open bay conditions, though Vela's on-site instructors run structured lessons for beginners too
description: Cabarete Bay is a genuine international meeting place for wing foilers — sailed here on three separate trips and met riders from the US, Canada, Europe, South America, and beyond. Local tip: Vela Watersports Center (https://velawatersportscabarete.com/), run by Jens — knowledgeable, helpful, a great guy — is a full-service shop for everything wing foiling related: gear rentals, lessons, on-site gear storage (so you don't have to haul your own gear from the hotel), and repairs. There's also a public parking lot just across the street, a couple pesos for a safe place to leave your car.
sourceNote: Firsthand-verified (2026-08-29) by Will. Coordinates updated to Will's own precise pin (2026-09-02).

name: Fort De Soto Park (East Beach)
waterType: Large shallow sandbar flats, 2-4 ft deep at high tide, protected by an offshore sandbar system roughly 1,400 ft out — can go glassy flat depending on tide
windDirection: NE, E, SE, S, and SSW all work well; NE is especially smooth thanks to wide-open fetch across the bay
description: A long-standing wing foil launch at the south end of Pinellas County, with a huge shallow sandbar system that keeps the water flat and forgiving across a wide range of wind directions. Good for a beginner's first flat-water sessions, while still holding interest for experienced riders on a bigger wind day. Watch for shells and oyster beds on the bottom (wear booties), muddy footing at low tide, fire ants near the rigging area, mangroves downwind of the launch, and paid parking with active ranger enforcement.

name: Doug's Beach
waterType: Columbia River, sandy bottom, wind swell and chop, deep water close to shore

description: About 20 minutes east of Hood River on Highway 14, a genuine Washington State Park and longtime windsurfing fixture increasingly drawing wing foilers chasing the same reliable thermal — a distinctly more advanced, more current-exposed scene than the more sheltered Hood River Event Site closer to town. Strong current can sweep a rider well across the river; no kite launching here at all (foil, wing, and windsurf only); requires a WA Discover Pass ($30) for parking.

description: One of the best-known Great Lakes wind-sports towns, home to MACkite Boardsports Center, which teaches wing foiling and eFoiling in town. Summer beach crowds make riding near shore tight in peak season — spring and fall are clearer; watch for pier and channel traffic.
